components.note: 屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.
氵 (water) — 活 relates to water flowing, a symbol of life and vitality.
舌 (shé) gives a hint of the sound — 活 is pronounced huó, a connection that has shifted over time.

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn xǐhuan xiànzài de shēnghuó.
example.english: I really like my life right now.
example.fact: 生活 refers to everyday living or lifestyle — how one spends one's days — and is a common false-friend trap for learners who reach for it to translate “life” in the biological sense; that meaning instead belongs to 生命, as in 生命危险 (“life-threatening danger”), never 生活危险.

components.note: 矢 (arrow) — 医 originally related to treating arrow wounds, the root of its meaning 'to cure, doctor'
匸 gives a loose sound connection to 医's reading yī
屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.

example.pinyin: Yīshēng shuō wǒ xūyào duō xiūxi.
example.english: The doctor said I need to rest more.
example.fact: 医 already meant “to cure” on its own (built from 矢, arrow — treating arrow wounds was one of medicine's earliest jobs) — 医生 literally reads as “one who cures the living,” pairing that cure-verb with 生 (“to live, life”).

components.note: 日 (sun) — 最 pictures something happening under the sun, that is, everywhere.
取 (to take, gather) — combined with the sun above, gathering everything under the sun gave 最 its meaning of 'most' or 'the utmost.'

example.pinyin: Zuìhòu, tā juédìng liú zài Běijīng.
example.english: In the end, he decided to stay in Beijing.
example.fact: 最后 typically opens a sentence as a transitional adverb (“finally, in the end”) summarizing a sequence, while directly before another noun (最后一天, “the last day”) it functions more like an ordinary adjective — one word covering both an English adverb and an adjective.

components.note: A stylized foot (related to 止, 'to stop/foot') — originally meant 'to go,' later grammaticalized into a literary possessive/linking particle, similar to 的.

example.pinyin: Shuìjiào zhīqián, wǒ xǐhuan kàn shū.
example.english: Before going to sleep, I like to read.
example.fact: 之前 almost always follows the event it's relative to, rather than preceding it the way English “before” does — Chinese says literally “sleep-before” (睡觉之前) where English says “before sleep,” a mirrored word order that trips up many learners building their first time clauses.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 伙 relates to people who share meals or work together.
火 (huǒ) gives the sound — an exact match with 伙's reading huǒ.
讠 (speech) — 计 relates to counting or planning through words and numbers.
十 (shí) gives a hint of the sound — 计 is pronounced jì, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.

example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒ zuì hǎo de huǒji.
example.english: He's my best partner.
example.fact: 伙计 combines 伙 (“companion, mate” — people who share meals or work together) with 计 (“to reckon, to plan”) — originally a business partner one “reckoned accounts” with, the word later slid down in register to also mean an ordinary shop hand or waiter.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 任 relates to a person taking on a responsibility or role.
壬 (rén) gives a hint of the sound — 任 is pronounced rèn, a connection that has shifted somewhat.

example.hanzi: 任何人都可以参加这个活动。
example.pinyin: Rènhé rén dōu kěyǐ cānjiā zhège huódòng.
example.english: Anyone can take part in this activity.
example.fact: 任何 pairs naturally with 都 right after its noun (任何人都..., “anyone at all...”) — the same 都-reinforcement pattern seen in 什么都 and 谁都, turning a plain indefinite word into an emphatic “no matter which” statement.

components.note: 彳 (step, to walk) — an older, now faded connection tied to movement.
艮 (gèn) gives a hint of the sound — 很 is pronounced hěn, a connection that has drifted significantly over time.
夕 (evening/night), doubled — two nights stacked together suggested the idea of accumulation, giving 多 its meaning of 'many, much.'

example.pinyin: Gōngyuán lǐ yǒu hěnduō huā.
example.english: There are a lot of flowers in the park.
example.fact: 很多 stacks the intensifier 很 (“very”) directly onto 多 (“many, much”) — and unlike most nouns quantified with a plain number, 多 by itself can't easily stand as a complete predicate of quantity in a simple statement; it almost always needs 很 (or another degree word) in front of it to sound natural, the same pattern that makes bare 好 sound curt next to a fuller 很好.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — used when asking a question aloud
那 (nà) gives a sound close to 哪's reading nǎ, differing mainly in tone
儿 (simplified from 兒) depicts a small child, drawn with a large head on a small body — a simple picture of youth.

example.pinyin: Nǐ qù nǎr le?
example.english: Where did you go?
example.fact: 哪儿 is the Beijing/Mainland colloquial twin of 哪里 (also in this batch) — both mean “where,” but 哪儿 carries the same r-suffixed (儿化) flavor as 这儿/那儿, marking it as the more casual, spoken-register choice next to the neutral 哪里.

components.note: 禾 (grain/rice plant) — 种 relates to seeds and planting crops.
中 (zhōng) gives the sound — 种 is pronounced zhǒng, matching aside from tone.

example.hanzi: 我从来没见过这种颜色。
example.pinyin: Wǒ cónglái méi jiànguo zhèzhǒng yánsè.
example.english: I've never seen this kind of color before.
example.fact: 种 is Mandarin's default measure word for categories or types (“kind, sort”), not for physical objects — 这种 pairs the near-demonstrative 这 directly with that classifier the same way 一种, 那种, and 哪种 do, forming a small family of “type-of” phrases built on the same counter.

components.note: A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.
帝 depicts an altar stand used for sacrificial offerings to the gods — the one who presides over such rites came to be known as 帝, 'supreme ruler, emperor.'

example.hanzi: 很多人相信上帝的存在。
example.pinyin: Hěnduō rén xiāngxìn Shàngdì de cúnzài.
example.english: Many people believe in the existence of God.
example.fact: 上帝 combines 上 (“above, supreme”) with 帝 (“emperor” — originally the ruler who presided over ancestral sacrifice) into “the supreme ruler,” the term Chinese Bible translators adopted for the Christian and Judaic “God,” reusing a title that in ancient texts had also named the highest ancestral deity of the Shang dynasty.

components.note: 女 depicts a kneeling figure with arms crossed, a traditional posture — a simple picture of a woman.
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.pinyin: Nàge nǚrén shì wǒ de lǎoshī.
example.english: That woman is my teacher.
example.fact: 女人 names a woman in a generic, sometimes slightly blunt way (“a woman,” as opposed to a man), while the more formal, now near-universal polite term for addressing or referring respectfully to a woman is 女士 — swapping one for the other can noticeably shift a sentence's register.

components.note: 夕 (evening, night) — in the dark, one could not see a person's face, so calling out their name was necessary to identify them.
口 (mouth) — calling out with the mouth at night gave 名 its meaning 'name.'
宀 (a house) — the setting for the scene.
子 (a child) — a child inside the house, perhaps evoking a name being nurtured, the source of 字's meaning 'character, word; courtesy name.'

example.pinyin: Nǐ de míngzi jiào shénme?
example.english: What's your name?
example.fact: 名, per its own etymology, pictures calling out with the mouth (口) in the dark of night (夕) — a reminder that a name's oldest job was simply making yourself identifiable when you couldn't be seen. 字 adds the sense of a fixed, written-down designation, so together 名字 reads as “the name, spoken and set down.”

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 认 relates to recognizing or acknowledging something, often expressed through words.
人 (rén) gives the sound — 认 is pronounced rèn, a close variant of the same sound.
讠 (speech) — relates to 识's meaning 'to know, recognize,' knowledge conveyed through words.
只 (zhǐ) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from shí.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen shì qùnián rènshi de.
example.english: We got to know each other last year.
example.fact: This deck's pilot batch already flagged the 知道/认识 distinction at rank 3: 知道 covers knowing a fact, while 认识 — this word — is needed for knowing a person or place. 认识 has a further sense with no single-word English equivalent: recognizing a written character on sight, as in 你认识这个字吗? (“do you recognize this character?”).

components.note: 亼 — traditionally linked to an image of gathering or covering; its original pictorial sense has become obscure, but the character came to mean 'now, the present.'
日 (sun) — the sun is what disappears as evening falls
免 (to escape, avoid) — pictured as the sun slipping away, giving 晚 its sense of 'late, evening'

example.pinyin: Jīnwǎn wǒmen yìqǐ chīfàn ba.
example.english: Let's eat together tonight.
example.fact: 今晚 belongs to a tidy family of “今 + time-of-day” words — 今天 (today), 今早 (this morning), 今晚 (tonight) — all built by prefixing 今 (“this, now”) directly onto a time-of-day noun, with no preposition needed the way English needs “this.”

components.note: 亻 (person) plus 也 (also/additionally) — historically meant 'another person,' which developed into the third-person pronoun 'he/him.'

example.hanzi: 除了英语,他还会说其他语言。
example.pinyin: Chúle Yīngyǔ, tā hái huì shuō qítā yǔyán.
example.english: Besides English, he can also speak other languages.
example.fact: 其他 and its near-twin 其它 are written with different second characters (他 “he/other person” vs 它 “it, inanimate other”) but pronounced identically and used interchangeably in practice — mainland style guides now generally recommend 其他 for both people and things, letting the once-meaningful distinction fade.

components.note: 讠 (speech/writing) — the act of putting words down.
己 (oneself, private) — writing down one's own private notes or memories, giving 记 its meaning 'to record, remember.'
寸 (a hand) reaching for 旦 (originally 貝, a shell used as currency) — a picture of grasping something valuable, hence 'to obtain, to get.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ bú jìde tā de míngzi le.
example.english: I don't remember his name anymore.
example.fact: 记得 is negated with 不 rather than 没 (不记得, never 没记得) even though it describes a memory state rather than a discrete action — a reminder that 没 generally negates completed events or existence, while 不 negates ongoing states, habits, and abilities.

components.note: 宀 (roof) — 家 is about a home, the space under a roof.
豕 (shǐ, 'pig') supplies the ancient sound for 家; keeping a pig under one's roof was also a practical sign of a household in ancient China, though the modern readings jiā and shǐ no longer rhyme.
亻 (person) — 伙 relates to people who share meals or work together.
火 (huǒ) gives the sound — an exact match with 伙's reading huǒ.

example.pinyin: Zhège jiāhuo zǒngshì chídào.
example.english: This guy is always late.
example.fact: 家伙 literally started out meaning “household gear” — pots, tools, furniture, even livestock, anything kept “at home” (家) as a working “companion” (伙), senses still listed in its dictionary entry — before it drifted into today's dominant colloquial sense, a casual, often faintly disrespectful “guy” or “fellow.”

components.note: 戈 (a spear or weapon) — 或 pictures defending a territory.
口 (here representing a walled area or territory) — defending one's territory with a weapon gave 或 its early sense of 'a certain place,' which later shifted to mean 'or,' offering an alternative.

example.hanzi: 你可以喝茶,或者喝咖啡。
example.pinyin: Nǐ kěyǐ hē chá, huòzhě hē kāfēi.
example.english: You can drink tea, or drink coffee.
example.fact: 或者 connects statements — a genuine choice being offered or described (“A or B”) — while its close relative 还是 is reserved for actual yes/no questions (“A or B?”); mixing the two up is one of the most common structural slips intermediate learners make.

components.note: 辶 (to walk/move) — shows 过's core meaning of 'passing through' or 'crossing'
咼 (guō) gives a sound close to 过's reading guò; the simplified form 过 now uses 寸 in place of 咼, but the phonetic connection traces back to the traditional character 過

example.pinyin: Guòqù, zhèlǐ shì yí piàn nóngtián.
example.english: In the past, this used to be farmland.
example.fact: 过去 does triple duty: a noun for “the past” (在过去, “in the past”), a verb meaning “to pass by, go over” (走过去, “walk over there”), and, attached after another verb, a directional complement meaning motion away from the speaker (拿过去, “take it over there”) — three grammatical roles riding on the same two characters.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — used when asking a question aloud
那 (nà) gives a sound close to 哪's reading nǎ, differing mainly in tone
田 (farmland) over 土 (earth/soil) — originally referred to a village or a measured unit of farmland, later extended to mean 'inside' or a unit of distance.

example.pinyin: Nǐ de bāo zài nǎlǐ?
example.english: Where's your bag?
example.fact: Said twice in a row as a stock reply — “哪里哪里” — 哪里 turns into an almost automatic way to deflect a compliment (“oh, not at all,” literally “where, where?”) rather than asking a real question, a politeness convention with no literal English equivalent.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 担 relates to carrying something, often on a shoulder pole
旦 (dàn) gives a sound close to 担's reading dān, sharing a similar historical pronunciation
心 was originally a pictograph of the physical shape of a human heart, and came to represent the mind, feelings, and intention as well.

example.pinyin: Bié dānxīn, yíqiè dōu huì hǎo de.
example.english: Don't worry, everything will be fine.
example.fact: 担 on its own means “to carry, to shoulder” (as in carrying a load on a shoulder pole) — 担心 pictures worry as a weight literally shouldered on the 心 (“heart, mind”), the same image English draws on with “a load off my mind” or “carrying a worry.”

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) — 继 relates to continuing a thread without a break
米 (mǐ) gives a sound distantly related to 继's reading jì, reflecting sound change over a long time
纟 (thread) — 续 relates to continuing, like an unbroken thread
卖 (mài) gives a loose sound connection to 续's reading xù

example.pinyin: Qǐng dàjiā jìxù gōngzuò.
example.english: Please everyone continue working.
example.fact: 继 and 续 are near-synonyms doubled into one word — both independently mean “to continue, to carry on an unbroken thread,” continuing the same 纟 (“thread”) imagery visible in both characters' own components — the same reinforcement strategy behind 喜欢 and 应该, elsewhere in this deck.

components.note: 女 depicts a kneeling figure with arms crossed, a traditional posture — a simple picture of a woman.
子 (child) — 孩 relates directly to children
亥 (hài) gives a sound close to 孩's reading hái

example.hanzi: 那个女孩在公园里跳舞。
example.pinyin: Nàge nǚhái zài gōngyuán lǐ tiàowǔ.
example.english: That girl is dancing in the park.
example.fact: 女孩 is the casual, everyday counterpart to the more formal or bookish 女孩子 and 姑娘 — in spoken Mandarin, 女孩(儿) is usually the default choice for “girl,” with an optional 儿-suffix common in Beijing-area speech.

components.note: 木 (tree) — traditionally read as a tree that has borne fruit.
立 (standing) — standing close by to watch it grow, evoking closeness and nurture, extended to 亲's meaning 'close, dear; parent, relative.'
冖 (a roof/house) — the home being welcomed into.
友 (a friend) — brought close into one's home; the traditional form 愛 also includes 心 ('heart') in the middle — the source of 爱's meaning 'to love.'

example.pinyin: Qīn'ài de, nǐ huílai le!
example.english: Darling, you're back!
example.fact: 亲爱 almost never stands alone as a plain adjective — it shows up overwhelmingly in the fixed form 亲爱的, used both as a term of endearment addressing someone directly and, in more formal writing, as the salutation opening a letter (“Dear ___”).

meanings: (indicates continuation from the past towards us)

components.note: A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.
Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.pinyin: Tā mànmàn zuò le xiàlai.
example.english: He slowly sat down.
example.fact: 下来 is one of Mandarin's most productive direction-plus-result suffixes: literally “down + come,” it attaches after action verbs to mark downward movement toward the speaker (坐下来, “sit down”) but also extends abstractly to mark a state settling into place (安静下来, “to quiet down”) — a single suffix spanning both the literal and the metaphorical.

components.note: 乂 depicts a hand gripping a tool.
八 here depicts a hand-axe — a father shown wielding a tool to provide for and protect the family gave 父 its meaning 'father.'
木 (tree) — traditionally read as a tree that has borne fruit.
立 (standing) — standing close by to watch it grow, evoking closeness and nurture, extended to 亲's meaning 'close, dear; parent, relative.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ fùqīn shì yì míng yīshēng.
example.english: My father is a doctor.
example.fact: 父亲 is the formal, written-register word for “father” — built from 父 (traditionally read as a hand gripping a tool, evoking a father wielding it to provide for the family) plus 亲 (“close kin”) — while everyday spoken Mandarin overwhelmingly prefers the more casual 爸爸 when addressing or talking about one's own dad.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yǐqián zhù zài Shànghǎi.
example.english: I used to live in Shanghai.
example.fact: 以前 and 之前 (rank 104, also in this batch) are near-synonyms for “before,” but 以前 more often stands alone as a free-floating time word (“in the past, before now”), while 之前 more typically attaches directly after a specific clause or noun (X之前, “before X”) — a subtle distributional difference two words that translate the same in English don't reveal.

components.note: 羊 (sheep; here representing feathers or ornaments on a headdress) — an elaborate decoration worn on the head.
大 (a person, arms outstretched) — a person wearing a decorated headdress was seen as beautiful, giving 美 its meaning 'beautiful.'
囗 (a boundary/enclosure) surrounding 玉 (jade, treasure) — a country pictured as protected, valuable territory.

example.pinyin: Tā qùnián bāndào le Měiguó.
example.english: He moved to the US last year.
example.fact: A common explanation for 美国 is that it's a phonetic-plus-flattering transliteration of “America” — 美 was chosen partly for its sound (Měi echoing “Ame-”) and partly because 美 independently means “beautiful,” following the same pattern used to coin other country names, as in 英国 (“hero-nation,” England) and 德国 (“virtue-nation,” Germany).

components.note: 宀 (roof/house) — relates to 完's meaning 'complete, finish,' as in a fully built house.
元 (yuán) was the phonetic base; the pronunciation later shifted to wán, so only a partial rhyme remains today.
入 (enter, put away) — 全 pictures something being placed into safekeeping.
玉 (jade) — a valuable treasure kept whole and undamaged, giving 全 its meaning of 'complete' or 'entire.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ wánquán tóngyì nǐ de kànfǎ.
example.english: I completely agree with your view.
example.fact: 完全 works as both an adjective (“complete, whole”) describing a noun and an adverb (“completely, totally”) modifying a verb or adjective without changing form at all — placement in the sentence, not any suffix, is what signals which role it's playing.

components.note: 宀 (a roof) — a house where valuables are kept
玉 (jade) — the treasure kept safe inside
The character traces the rounded shell and radiating lines of a cowrie shell, once used as ancient Chinese currency.

example.hanzi: 这幅画是他最珍贵的宝贝。
example.pinyin: Zhè fú huà shì tā zuì zhēnguì de bǎobèi.
example.english: This painting is his most treasured possession.
example.fact: 贝 is a pictograph of a cowrie shell, once used as currency in ancient China — 宝贝 layers a second “treasure” character (宝, valuables kept under a roof) directly on top of it, so the word for a literal treasured object doubles as Mandarin's most common affectionate term for a baby or loved one, much like English “treasure” or “precious.”

components.note: 丁 (a stylized handle/hook shape in the ancient form) — part of the character's original picture, now mostly opaque in the modern form
口 (kǒu, mouth) gives a sound related to 可's pronunciation kě, and may connect to 可's sense of approval spoken aloud
Traditionally analyzed as 日 combined with 疋, linked to the idea of speaking directly and truthfully — the source of 是's meaning 'to be, indeed, right.'

example.hanzi: 我很想去,可是没有时间。
example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn xiǎng qù, kěshì méiyǒu shíjiān.
example.english: I really want to go, but I don't have time.
example.fact: 可是 was already flagged at rank 18 of this deck's pilot batch (但是) as sitting a shade more conversational than the neutral 但是 — of Mandarin's three common “but” words, 可是 leans spoken and slightly emphatic, 但是 is the neutral default, and 不过 is the softest, most casual of the three.

components.note: 世 depicts three leaves or shoots on a stem, suggesting continuous growth across generations — giving rise to the meaning 'generation' or 'world.'
田 (field) — relates to 界's original meaning, the boundary line between farm fields.
介 (jiè) gives the sound — 界 is also pronounced jiè, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng qù kànkan zhège shìjiè.
example.english: I want to go see the world.
example.fact: 世, per its own character-card etymology, depicts three leaves or shoots stacked on a stem — a picture of successive generations growing one atop another — and 界 separately contributes “boundary” (from 田, the line between fields); 世界 literally reads as “the bounded span of generations,” an unexpectedly poetic origin for today's plain word “world.”

components.note: 八 (to divide/split) — represents something being separated into smaller parts.
亅 (a hook/line) — cutting a small piece off, an image tied to the meaning 'small, tiny.'
日 (sun/day) — relates to 时's meaning of 'time, season'; the phonetic part of the character was later replaced by 寸 in the simplified form

example.hanzi: 这趟火车要开三个小时。
example.pinyin: Zhè tàng huǒchē yào kāi sān gè xiǎoshí.
example.english: This train ride takes three hours.
example.fact: 小时 literally means “small hour” — 时 alone already meant a broader unit of time (as in 时候, also in this deck's pilot batch), and prefixing 小 narrowed it down specifically to the 24th-of-a-day measure borrowed from the Western clock, distinct from 时辰, the older 2-hour unit traditional Chinese timekeeping used.

components.note: 千 (thousand) — 重 pictures a heavy burden carried a great distance.
里 (a unit of distance, like a mile) — carrying something a thousand 里 emphasizes how heavy and significant a burden it is, giving 重 its meaning 'heavy' or 'important.'
女 (woman) with 覀 depicting hands on the waist — an old image of insisting or demanding something, connected to 要's meaning 'to want, to need.'

example.pinyin: Jiànkāng bǐ shénme dōu zhòngyào.
example.english: Health is more important than anything.
example.fact: 重 is a heteronym: read zhòng it means “heavy” or “important” (as here), but read chóng the same character means “to repeat, again” (as in 重复) — two unrelated jobs split across one character by pronunciation alone.

components.note: 另 (other, separate) — 别 relates to distinguishing one thing from another.
刂 (knife) — cutting things apart to sort them gave 别 its meaning 'to separate' or 'other,' and later, 'don't' as a command.
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.pinyin: Bú yào zǒngshì hé biéren bǐjiào.
example.english: Don't always compare yourself to other people.
example.fact: 别 carries two unrelated jobs that both show up in this deck: as 别人's “other, separate” (from cutting things apart with a 刂 knife), and — completely independently — as a bare command meaning “don't” (别说, “don't say it”), a shortening of 不要 that has nothing to do with “separateness” at all.

components.note: 田 (field) — represents farmland.
力 (strength/effort) — someone strong enough to work the fields gave 男 its meaning 'male, man.'
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.pinyin: Nàge nánrén zài xiū zìxíngchē.
example.english: That man is fixing a bicycle.
example.fact: 男 is one of Mandarin's more transparent compositional characters: 田 (“field”) stacked over 力 (“strength, muscular effort”) pictures exactly the ancient division of labor the word encodes — a man was, by this character's logic, defined as the one strong enough to work the fields.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 机 originally referred to a wooden device or machine, such as a loom.
几 depicts a small table or stool — combined with 木 (wood), the character pictured a wooden machine or mechanism.
人 (people) over 云 (clouds/say) — a picture of people gathering and speaking together, related to 会's meanings 'to meet' and 'to know how to.'

example.pinyin: Zhè shì yí gè hěn hǎo de jīhuì.
example.english: This is a very good opportunity.
example.fact: 机 originally meant a mechanical device or trigger mechanism (from 木 “wood” plus 几, an old stool or table shape suggesting a wooden contraption) — 机会 pairs that “trigger” sense with 会 (“a meeting, a coming-together”) into something like “the moment the mechanism clicks into place,” a vivid image behind the everyday word for “opportunity.”

components.note: 屮 (a young sprout) growing up and out of 凵 (a container or pit) — a picture of something emerging, hence 'going out.'

example.hanzi: 外面在下雨,你还要出去吗?
example.pinyin: Wàimiàn zài xiàyǔ, nǐ hái yào chūqù ma?
example.english: It's raining outside, do you still want to go out?
example.fact: 出去 combines two directional verbs — 出 (“to exit, emerge”) and 去 (“to go,” moving away from the speaker) — into a single compound that, like 出来 and 进去, packs both the direction of motion and its relation to the speaker's position into one word, a category English usually splits across separate prepositions.

components.note: 手 (hand) — depicts a hand raised above the eyes.
目 (eye) — shielding the eyes with a hand to look into the distance gave 看 its meaning 'to look, to see.'
冂 (a simplified eye shape in 见's modern form) — emphasizes the act of seeing.
儿 (a person) — a person with an emphasized eye above gives 见 its meaning 'to see.'

example.hanzi: 我在路上看见了你的朋友。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zài lùshang kànjiàn le nǐ de péngyou.
example.english: I saw your friend on the road.
example.fact: 看 alone means the deliberate act of looking, but doesn't guarantee anything registered — attaching 见 (“to perceive”) as a result complement turns it into 看见, “to look and successfully perceive,” the same success-complement pattern behind 听见 (“to hear,” listen + perceive) and 找到 (“to find,” search + arrive-at-a-result).

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 打 relates to hitting or performing an action with the hand.
丁 (dīng) gives the sound — 打 is pronounced dǎ, a connection that has shifted in tone.
电 (simplified from 電) depicts a bolt of lightning — since lightning is a natural form of electricity, the character came to mean 'electricity.'
讠 (speech) — 话 relates to speaking and words.
舌 (tongue) — the organ used for speaking, reinforcing 话's meaning of 'speech' or 'words.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ míngtiān gěi nǐ dǎ diànhuà.
example.english: I'll call you tomorrow.
example.fact: 打 is one of Mandarin's most overloaded verbs of “impact, action” — literally “to hit,” it extends metaphorically into dozens of set collocations with nothing to do with striking, including 打电话 (“make a call”), 打的 (“hail a taxi”), and 打扫 (“to clean”), each pairing 打 with a different object to produce an unrelated action.

components.note: 女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'
亻 (person) — relates to 像's meaning 'to resemble, be like; image, portrait,' comparing one person or thing to another.
象 (xiàng) gives the sound — 像 is also pronounced xiàng, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā hǎoxiàng bú tài gāoxìng.
example.english: He doesn't seem too happy.
example.fact: 好像 softens a claim into a guess or impression (“it seems as if...”) and, unlike English “seem,” can open a sentence on its own with no dummy subject needed — 好像要下雨了 (“it looks like it's going to rain”) has no equivalent of English's placeholder “it.”

components.note: 寸 (a hand) reaching for 旦 (originally 貝, a shell used as currency) — a picture of grasping something valuable, hence 'to obtain, to get.'
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.hanzi: 他的努力终于得到了回报。
example.pinyin: Tā de nǔlì zhōngyú dédào le huíbào.
example.english: His hard work finally got rewarded.
example.fact: 得到 pairs 得 (“to obtain” — a hand reaching for a valuable shell, per its own etymology) with 到 (“to arrive, to reach”) into “obtaining by reaching” — while its plain root 得 alone can also act as a purely grammatical particle in other contexts (记得, 觉得, both elsewhere in this deck) with no “obtaining” sense left at all.

components.note: 言 (speech) — 警 relates to speaking out a warning or alarm
敬 (jìng) gives a sound close to 警's reading jǐng, sharing a similar historical pronunciation
宀 (roof) — 察 relates to careful observation
祭 (jì) gives a loose sound connection to 察's reading chá

example.hanzi: 警察正在调查这起案件。
example.pinyin: Jǐngchá zhèngzài diàochá zhè qǐ ànjiàn.
example.english: The police are investigating this case.
example.fact: 警 and 察 are near-synonyms doubled together — 警 carries “to warn, to alert” (built from 言, speech) and 察 carries “to observe closely, to inspect” (built from 宀, a roof, evoking careful indoor scrutiny) — combining “alertness” with “close observation” into the job description behind “police.”

components.note: 儿 (simplified from 兒) depicts a small child, drawn with a large head on a small body — a simple picture of youth.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 他们的儿子已经上大学了。
example.pinyin: Tāmen de érzi yǐjīng shàng dàxué le.
example.english: Their son is already in college.
example.fact: 儿 on its own is a pictograph of a small child (a big head over a small body) and separately doubles as Mandarin's diminutive r-suffix (儿化, as in 这儿, “here”) — 儿子 keeps 儿's original “child” meaning intact, distinguishing it from that purely phonetic suffix use.

meanings: (at the beginning of a sentence) afterwards

components.note: A stylized foot (related to 止, 'to stop/foot') — originally meant 'to go,' later grammaticalized into a literary possessive/linking particle, similar to 的.

example.hanzi: 下课之后,我们去打篮球。
example.pinyin: Xiàkè zhīhòu, wǒmen qù dǎ lánqiú.
example.english: After class, let's go play basketball.
example.fact: 之后 mirrors 之前 (rank 104, also in this batch) as its exact opposite — both attach after the event they're relative to (X之后/之前) rather than before it the way English “after X” / “before X” do, so the two form a matched pair of time-relation markers built the same way.

components.note: 氵 (water) reflects 漂's original meaning "to float, drift," though its most common modern use (in 漂亮) has drifted from that sense.
票 (piào) gives the exact sound for this reading of 漂, as in 漂亮 (piàoliang).
亮 is traditionally read as a picture of a lit oil lamp raised on a stand, radiating light — a fitting image for its meaning 'bright, radiant.'

example.hanzi: 她今天穿的裙子很漂亮。
example.pinyin: Tā jīntiān chuān de qúnzi hěn piàoliang.
example.english: The skirt she's wearing today is very pretty.
example.fact: 漂 carries multiple readings depending on the word: piāo means “to float, drift” (its most common reading, as in 漂浮), piǎo means “to bleach” (漂白), and piào is reserved specifically for 漂亮 — a reminder that a whole word's pronunciation can diverge from a character's default reading, tripping up learners who default to piāoliang.

components.note: 八 (to divide/split apart) — represents something already split into parts.
刀 (knife) — a knife cutting already-divided pieces further, giving 分 its meaning 'to divide, to separate.'
钅 (metal) — clocks and bells like 钟 were traditionally made of metal.
中 (zhōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 钟.

example.hanzi: 电影再过十分钟就开始了。
example.pinyin: Diànyǐng zài guò shí fēnzhōng jiù kāishǐ le.
example.english: The movie starts in ten more minutes.
example.fact: 钟 literally means “bell” or, by extension, “clock” (bells and later clocks were traditionally made of metal, hence the 钅 radical) — 分钟 literally reads as “a divided portion (分) of the clock (钟),” a compositional logic that mirrors English “minute” coming from Latin “minutus,” a “small” division of the hour.

components.note: 再 depicts something stacked again on top of a base line — repetition, or doing something 'once more,' is pictured by piling on an extra layer.
冂 (a simplified eye shape in 见's modern form) — emphasizes the act of seeing.
儿 (a person) — a person with an emphasized eye above gives 见 its meaning 'to see.'

example.pinyin: Hǎo de, zàijiàn!
example.english: Okay, goodbye!
example.fact: 再见 is literally “see (you) again” — 再 (“once more, again”) plus 见 (“to see”) — making it structurally closer to French “au revoir” or Spanish “hasta la vista” than to English “goodbye,” which instead comes from a contraction of “God be with ye.”

components.note: 女 (woman) — depicts a wife in the traditional image behind this character.
口 (mouth/words) — the wife following her husband's spoken words gave 如 its meaning of 'as, like, if.'

example.hanzi: 我们应该如何解决这个问题?
example.pinyin: Wǒmen yīnggāi rúhé jiějué zhège wèntí?
example.english: How should we solve this problem?
example.fact: 如何 is the more formal, written-register cousin of 怎么样 — mentioned in this deck's pilot batch (rank 9) as the casual, spoken way to ask “how is X” — with 如何 dominating essays, news reports, and official questions, while 怎么样 rules everyday conversation.

components.note: 比 is made of two identical 匕 (spoon) shapes placed side by side — comparing two similar things led to its meaning 'to compare.'
贝 (shell, an ancient form of money) — 赛 originally related to offering valuables, later coming to mean 'to compete.'
宀 (mián) gives a sound distantly related to sài, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 明天有一场重要的比赛。
example.pinyin: Míngtiān yǒu yì chǎng zhòngyào de bǐsài.
example.english: There's an important match tomorrow.
example.fact: 赛 relates to offering up valuables (built from 贝, shell-money), likely tied to ancient wager or prize customs, and 比 contributes “to compare” (two identical 匕 spoon-shapes side by side) — together 比赛 literally suggests “comparing while something valuable is at stake.”
